title: Community Drivers of Leishmania Infections Transmission and Control in Baringo County, Kenya: Implications for Integrated One Health Intervention Strategies
content:
Leishmaniasis is an endemic zoonotic disease caused by protozoan parasite Leishmania and transmitted through bites of infected female phlebotomine sandflies. It is listed by the World Health Organization (WHO) as one of the 20 neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), ranking ninth globally. The disease affects resource-poor populations in tropical regions. Kenya is one of the endemic countries with the highest global burden of leishmaniasis with Baringo County being a major endemic focus.  
A cross-sectional KAP survey was conducted between July 2025 and January 2026 among 135 residents of Baringo South Sub-County using a structured questionnaire. The study assessed sociodemographic characteristics, awareness of the disease, perception, preventive practices. The perception of the residents on treatment-seeking behaviors was evaluated regarding leishmaniasis in Baringo County. About 12 healthcare professionals were also interviewed regarding their diagnostic and treatment capacity of healthcare provision in the region. Associations between variables were examined using multivariate logistic
 regressions.
The overall awareness of leishmaniasis was high (94.8%) with Knowledge, attitudes, and practices scores as 86.7%, 76%, and 77.7% respectively. However, critical knowledge gaps on transmission dynamics, the role of role of dogs as reservoir hosts and preventive practices remained incomplete. Significant associations were observed for awareness of local cases, recognition of clinical signs, knowledge of vector activity, community control measures and attitude towards treatment preferences. Age and education levels were predictors of KAP. Health care practitioners demonstrated technical diagnostic and treatment capacity of human Leishmania infections while the veterinarians were not aware of the leishmania infection in dogs and its diagnoses and treatment. Therefore, the integration of human, animal, and vector surveillance within a One Health framework is essential to strengthen disease monitoring and control.
